raw_evidence.label: Sherman Kent and the 'serious possibility' problem
raw_evidence.content: The core problem this dataset probes is decades old. In 1951 a US National Intelligence Estimate said there was a 'serious possibility' of a Soviet attack on Yugoslavia. When CIA analyst Sherman Kent — later called the 'father of intelligence analysis' — polled colleagues on what 'serious possibility' meant numerically, answers ranged from a 20% chance to an 80% chance for the very same phrase. Kent's 1964 essay 'Words of Estimative Probability' argued that verbal probability terms are dangerously ambiguous and proposed a fixed scale mapping words to numbers (e.g. 'probable' = 75% ±12%, 'almost certain' = 93% ±6%, 'chances about even' = 50%). The Kucharski quiz is essentially a crowd-sourced, 5,000-person rerun of Kent's experiment.

raw_evidence.label: Official scales: Kent, NIC, IPCC
raw_evidence.content: Several institutions have tried to standardise probability words. Kent's CIA scale: certain 100%, almost certain ~93%, probable ~75%, chances about even ~50%, probably not ~30%, almost certainly not ~7%, impossible 0%. The IPCC climate scale: 'virtually certain' >99%, 'very likely' >90%, 'likely' >66%, 'about as likely as not' 33–66%, 'unlikely' <33%, 'very unlikely' <10%. UK intelligence (the Professional Head of Intelligence Assessment 'probability yardstick') officially defines 'realistic possibility' as 40–50%. These provide external benchmarks against which the crowd's interpretations can be measured — and against which disagreement can be quantified.

raw_evidence.label: 'Realistic Possibility' vs the official 40–50%
raw_evidence.content: UK intelligence officially defines 'realistic possibility' as a 40–50% likelihood. The crowd disagrees wildly: only 17.5% of responses landed inside that 40–50% band. Far more (64.0%) placed it above 50%, and 18.5% put it below 40%. The mean was 57.0 and the median 60 — both above the official ceiling. Estimates filled the entire 0–100 range, with a clear peak around 60–70%. In other words, the phrase that a government uses to mean 'a bit less than even' is read by most people as 'better than even'. It is the dataset's sharpest illustration of why a single estimative word cannot safely carry a decision.

raw_evidence.label: Origin: Kucharski's CAPphrase quiz
raw_evidence.content: The dataset comes from an online quiz titled 'How likely is ‘likely’?' created as an independent side project by epidemiologist and mathematician Adam Kucharski (London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine). Participants did two tasks: (1) they typed a numeric value from 0–100% for each of 19 common probability phrases (the 'absolute judgements'), and (2) they were shown pairs of phrases and asked which conveyed a higher probability (the 'pairwise comparisons'), seeing 10 pairs each — 9 unique plus 1 repeated pair as an internal consistency check. The released CAPphrase dataset (Comparative and Absolute Probability phrase) contains responses from 5,174 participants and over 150,000 individual language judgements, and is open-access with a DOI (10.5281/zenodo.18750055). It was featured as the TidyTuesday dataset for 2026-03-10, curated by Nicola Rennie.

raw_evidence.label: Which words people disagree on most
raw_evidence.content: Ranking phrases by the standard deviation of their estimates reveals where consensus collapses. 'Realistic Possibility' is the single most contested word, with a std of 20.5 and an interquartile range of 35 points (40 to 75) — people genuinely cannot agree what it means. The three modal verbs 'Could Happen' (18.2), 'Might Happen' (17.7) and 'May Happen' (17.0) follow close behind. At the other end, agreement is tightest where the words are most absolute: 'About Even' (3.7), 'Almost Certain' (5.8), 'Almost No Chance' (6.0), 'Will Happen' (6.9). The pattern is clean: disagreement peaks in the murky middle and around hedge words, and vanishes at the certain extremes — exactly the shape every formal study since Sherman Kent has found.

rp = aj[aj.term == 'Realistic Possibility']['probability']
in_band = ((rp >= 40) & (rp <= 50)).mean() * 100
raw_evidence.output: Realistic Possibility std 20.5 (iqr 35); Could Happen 18.2; Might Happen 17.7; May Happen 17.0; Highly Unlikely 12.4; Probable 12.0; ... About Even 3.7; Almost Certain 5.8; Almost No Chance 6.0; Will Happen 6.9

raw_evidence.label: People are 96.6% consistent with themselves
raw_evidence.content: Every respondent saw one pair twice as a hidden consistency check. When the same two phrases came back around, 96.6% of people chose the same winner both times; only 3.4% (174 of 5,174) flipped their answer. So the wild disagreement in this data is not noise inside each head — individuals are remarkably stable. The variance is between people, not within them: we each have a firm private sense of what 'likely' means, and the problem is that those private senses don't match.

raw_evidence.label: Origin: Kucharski's CAPphrase quiz
raw_evidence.content: The dataset comes from an online quiz titled 'How likely is ‘likely’?' created as an independent side project by epidemiologist and mathematician Adam Kucharski (London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine). Participants did two tasks: (1) they typed a numeric value from 0–100% for each of 19 common probability phrases (the 'absolute judgements'), and (2) they were shown pairs of phrases and asked which conveyed a higher probability (the 'pairwise comparisons'), seeing 10 pairs each — 9 unique plus 1 repeated pair as an internal consistency check. The released CAPphrase dataset (Comparative and Absolute Probability phrase) contains responses from 5,174 participants and over 150,000 individual language judgements, and is open-access with a DOI (10.5281/zenodo.18750055). It was featured as the TidyTuesday dataset for 2026-03-10, curated by Nicola Rennie.

raw_evidence.label: Which words people disagree on most
raw_evidence.content: Ranking phrases by the standard deviation of their estimates reveals where consensus collapses. 'Realistic Possibility' is the single most contested word, with a std of 20.5 and an interquartile range of 35 points (40 to 75) — people genuinely cannot agree what it means. The three modal verbs 'Could Happen' (18.2), 'Might Happen' (17.7) and 'May Happen' (17.0) follow close behind. At the other end, agreement is tightest where the words are most absolute: 'About Even' (3.7), 'Almost Certain' (5.8), 'Almost No Chance' (6.0), 'Will Happen' (6.9). The pattern is clean: disagreement peaks in the murky middle and around hedge words, and vanishes at the certain extremes — exactly the shape every formal study since Sherman Kent has found.

raw_evidence.label: People are 96.6% consistent with themselves
raw_evidence.content: Every respondent saw one pair twice as a hidden consistency check. When the same two phrases came back around, 96.6% of people chose the same winner both times; only 3.4% (174 of 5,174) flipped their answer. So the wild disagreement in this data is not noise inside each head — individuals are remarkably stable. The variance is between people, not within them: we each have a firm private sense of what 'likely' means, and the problem is that those private senses don't match.

raw_evidence.label: Sherman Kent and the 'serious possibility' problem
raw_evidence.content: The core problem this dataset probes is decades old. In 1951 a US National Intelligence Estimate said there was a 'serious possibility' of a Soviet attack on Yugoslavia. When CIA analyst Sherman Kent — later called the 'father of intelligence analysis' — polled colleagues on what 'serious possibility' meant numerically, answers ranged from a 20% chance to an 80% chance for the very same phrase. Kent's 1964 essay 'Words of Estimative Probability' argued that verbal probability terms are dangerously ambiguous and proposed a fixed scale mapping words to numbers (e.g. 'probable' = 75% ±12%, 'almost certain' = 93% ±6%, 'chances about even' = 50%). The Kucharski quiz is essentially a crowd-sourced, 5,000-person rerun of Kent's experiment.

raw_evidence.label: Official scales: Kent, NIC, IPCC
raw_evidence.content: Several institutions have tried to standardise probability words. Kent's CIA scale: certain 100%, almost certain ~93%, probable ~75%, chances about even ~50%, probably not ~30%, almost certainly not ~7%, impossible 0%. The IPCC climate scale: 'virtually certain' >99%, 'very likely' >90%, 'likely' >66%, 'about as likely as not' 33–66%, 'unlikely' <33%, 'very unlikely' <10%. UK intelligence (the Professional Head of Intelligence Assessment 'probability yardstick') officially defines 'realistic possibility' as 40–50%. These provide external benchmarks against which the crowd's interpretations can be measured — and against which disagreement can be quantified.

raw_evidence.label: 'Realistic Possibility' vs the official 40–50%
raw_evidence.content: UK intelligence officially defines 'realistic possibility' as a 40–50% likelihood. The crowd disagrees wildly: only 17.5% of responses landed inside that 40–50% band. Far more (64.0%) placed it above 50%, and 18.5% put it below 40%. The mean was 57.0 and the median 60 — both above the official ceiling. Estimates filled the entire 0–100 range, with a clear peak around 60–70%. In other words, the phrase that a government uses to mean 'a bit less than even' is read by most people as 'better than even'. It is the dataset's sharpest illustration of why a single estimative word cannot safely carry a decision.

raw_evidence.label: Sherman Kent and the 'serious possibility' problem
raw_evidence.content: The core problem this dataset probes is decades old. In 1951 a US National Intelligence Estimate said there was a 'serious possibility' of a Soviet attack on Yugoslavia. When CIA analyst Sherman Kent — later called the 'father of intelligence analysis' — polled colleagues on what 'serious possibility' meant numerically, answers ranged from a 20% chance to an 80% chance for the very same phrase. Kent's 1964 essay 'Words of Estimative Probability' argued that verbal probability terms are dangerously ambiguous and proposed a fixed scale mapping words to numbers (e.g. 'probable' = 75% ±12%, 'almost certain' = 93% ±6%, 'chances about even' = 50%). The Kucharski quiz is essentially a crowd-sourced, 5,000-person rerun of Kent's experiment.

raw_evidence.label: 'Realistic Possibility' vs the official 40–50%
raw_evidence.content: UK intelligence officially defines 'realistic possibility' as a 40–50% likelihood. The crowd disagrees wildly: only 17.5% of responses landed inside that 40–50% band. Estimates filled the entire 0–100 range, with a clear peak around 60–70%. It is the dataset's sharpest illustration of why a single estimative word cannot safely carry a decision.

raw_evidence.label: Related work: replicated academic findings
raw_evidence.content: Kucharski's crowd quiz sits in a long line of formal studies. A NATO study asked 23 officers (squadron leader to lieutenant general) to put numbers on probability words and found they did NOT use the Sherman Kent scale even when familiar with it. Academic work (e.g. the University of Illinois 'Perception of Probability Words' visualization, and survey studies) consistently finds wide between-person variance for mid-range terms and tighter agreement at the extremes ('certain', 'impossible'). This means the analyst's findings — if disagreement is largest in the middle and smallest at the ends — would confirm a robust, repeatedly observed pattern rather than a quirk of this one sample.

raw_evidence.label: Which words people disagree on most
raw_evidence.content: Ranking phrases by the standard deviation of their estimates reveals where consensus collapses. 'Realistic Possibility' is the single most contested word, with a std of 20.5 and an interquartile range of 35 points (40 to 75) — people genuinely cannot agree what it means. The three modal verbs 'Could Happen' (18.2), 'Might Happen' (17.7) and 'May Happen' (17.0) follow close behind. At the other end, agreement is tightest where the words are most absolute: 'About Even' (3.7), 'Almost Certain' (5.8), 'Almost No Chance' (6.0), 'Will Happen' (6.9). raw_evidence.content: In the pairwise task, some phrase match-ups are essentially coin flips. 'Improbable' vs 'Remote Chance' split 50.8/49.2, and 'Could Happen' vs 'Might Happen' split exactly the same 50.8/49.2 — the crowd has no shared sense of which is higher. 'Likely' vs 'Probable', the quiz's title fight, went 53.1% to Likely — close, but with a twist (see the flip below). 'Chances are Slight' vs 'Unlikely' (45.6/54.4) and vs 'Little Chance' (45.5/54.5) are nearly as tight. The closest contests cluster exactly among the high-disagreement phrases from the absolute task, confirming the two methods see the same fog from different angles.

return tuple(sorted([r['term1'], r['term2']]))
pc['pair'] = pc.apply(pair_key, axis=1)
rows = []
for pair, grp in pc.groupby('pair'):
    a, b = pair
    n = len(grp)
    a_wins = (grp['selected'] == a).sum()
    b_wins = (grp['selected'] == b).sum()
    # share that picked the alphabetically-first term
    a_share = a_wins / n * 100
    winner_share = max(a_wins, b_wins) / n * 100
    rows.append([a, b, n, a_wins, b_wins, round(a_share,1), round(winner_share,1)])
contests = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=['term_a','term_b','n','a_wins','b_wins','a_share','winner_share'])
closest = contests.sort_values('winner_share').head(12)

raw_evidence.label: Two methods agree — except where words tie
raw_evidence.content: The absolute ranking (by mean value) and the pairwise ranking (by win rate) agree almost perfectly, with a Spearman correlation of 0.989. raw_evidence.code:
for _, r in pc.iterrows():
    for t in [r['term1'], r['term2']]:

winrate = pd.Series({t: wins.get(t,0)/appear[t] for t in appear}).sort_values(ascending=False)
abs_rank = abs_mean.rank(ascending=False)
pw_rank = winrate.rank(ascending=False)
cmp = pd.DataFrame({'abs_mean': abs_mean, 'abs_rank': abs_rank, 'winrate': winrate*100, 'pw_rank': pw_rank})

cmp['rank_gap'] = cmp['abs_rank'] - cmp['pw_rank']
print(cmp.round(1).to_string())
sp = cmp[['abs_rank','pw_rank']].corr(method='spearman').iloc[0,1]
print(f"Spearman rank correlation (absolute vs pairwise): {sp:.3f}")

raw_evidence.label: The closest head-to-head contests
raw_evidence.content: In the pairwise task, some phrase match-ups are essentially coin flips. 'Improbable' vs 'Remote Chance' split 50.8/49.2, and 'Could Happen' vs 'Might Happen' split exactly the same 50.8/49.2 — the crowd has no shared sense of which is higher. 'Likely' vs 'Probable', the quiz's title fight, went 53.1% to Likely — close, but with a twist (see the flip below). 'Chances are Slight' vs 'Unlikely' (45.6/54.4) and vs 'Little Chance' (45.5/54.5) are nearly as tight. The closest contests cluster exactly among the high-disagreement phrases from the absolute task, confirming the two methods see the same fog from different angles.
raw_evidence.code:
return tuple(sorted([r['term1'], r['term2']]))
pc['pair'] = pc.apply(pair_key, axis=1)
rows = []
for pair, grp in pc.groupby('pair'):
    a, b = pair
    n = len(grp)
    a_wins = (grp['selected'] == a).sum()
    b_wins = (grp['selected'] == b).sum()

raw_evidence.content: Kucharski's crowd quiz sits in a long line of formal studies. A NATO study asked 23 officers (squadron leader to lieutenant general) to put numbers on probability words and found they did NOT use the Sherman Kent scale even when familiar with it. This means the analyst's findings — if disagreement is largest in the middle and smallest at the ends — would confirm a robust, repeatedly observed pattern rather than a quirk of this one sample.

raw_evidence.label: Sherman Kent and the 'serious possibility' problem
raw_evidence.content: The core problem this dataset probes is decades old. In 1951 a US National Intelligence Estimate said there was a 'serious possibility' of a Soviet attack on Yugoslavia. When CIA analyst Sherman Kent — later called the 'father of intelligence analysis' — polled colleagues on what 'serious possibility' meant numerically, answers ranged from a 20% chance to an 80% chance for the very same phrase. Kent's 1964 essay 'Words of Estimative Probability' argued that verbal probability terms are dangerously ambiguous and proposed a fixed scale mapping words to numbers (e.g. 'probable' = 75% ±12%, 'almost certain' = 93% ±6%, 'chances about even' = 50%). The Kucharski quiz is essentially a crowd-sourced, 5,000-person rerun of Kent's experiment.

When the same two phrases came back around, 96.6% of people chose the same winner both times; only 3.4% (174 of 5,174) flipped their answer. raw_evidence.content: The core problem this dataset probes is decades old. In 1951 a US National Intelligence Estimate said there was a 'serious possibility' of a Soviet attack on Yugoslavia. Kent's 1964 essay 'Words of Estimative Probability' argued that verbal probability terms are dangerously ambiguous and proposed a fixed scale mapping words to numbers (e.g. 'probable' = 75% ±12%, 'almost certain' = 93% ±6%, 'chances about even' = 50%). sentences.summary: det_04: Kucharski's own headline findings. Source: Insights from over 150,000 human judgements (Kucharski) (https://kucharski.substack.com/p/insights-from-over-150000-human-judgements) Facts: 'Realistic possibility' had the most variance across respondents; More than half of estimates were multiples of 10; nearly a third ended in 5; ~1 in 5 rounded all estimates

raw_evidence.label: Kucharski's own headline findings
raw_evidence.content: In his write-up, Kucharski reported several patterns the analysis should check against. 'Realistic possibility' showed the most variance — it 'meant a lot of different things to different people' despite the UK's official 40–50% definition. Respondents almost unanimously agreed 'almost no chance' is lower than 'will happen', but split nearly 50/50 on whether 'could happen' or 'might happen' is higher. People love round numbers: more than half of all absolute estimates were multiples of 10, nearly a third ended in 5, and about one in five participants rounded every single estimate. Demographic effects were real but small: Americans gave estimates ~1.03x higher than British respondents, age effects were minimal (55–64 gave ~0.97x vs the 35–44 reference). Kucharski himself questioned whether 1–3% differences, though statistically significant in such a large sample, matter in practice.

raw_evidence.label: The pull of round numbers
raw_evidence.content: People do not answer like calibrated instruments — they reach for round numbers. Of all 98,306 estimates, 53.6% were exact multiples of 10 and another 31.2% ended in 5, so 84.8% of every probability judgement in the dataset is a multiple of five. Only 15.2% used any other digit. The last-digit histogram is brutally spiky: '0' accounts for 53.6% of answers and '5' for 31.2%, while '4' appears just 0.5% of the time. This is the same anchoring-to-round-numbers bias seen in surveys everywhere, and it means much of the apparent precision in these numbers is an illusion.
raw_evidence.code:
p = aj['probability']
mult10 = (p % 10 == 0).mean() * 100
end5 = (p % 10 == 5).mean() * 100
print(f"Multiples of 10: {mult10:.1f}%")
print(f"Ending in 5 (not 10): {end5:.1f}%")
print(f"Multiple of 5 (incl 10): {(p%5==0).mean()*100:.1f}%")
print(f"Other (not multiple of 5): {(p%5!=0).mean()*100:.1f}%")
# last-digit distribution for chart
ld = (p % 10).value_counts().sort_index()
print("last-digit counts:")
for d, c in ld.items():
    print(f"  {d}: {c} ({c/len(p)*100:.1f}%)")

# --- ana_06: Share of respondents who rounded EVERY estimate to a multiple of 10 ---
print("=== ana_06 ===")
def all_mult10(s): return (s % 10 == 0).all()
per_resp = aj.groupby('response_id')['probability'].apply(all_mult10)
print(f"Respondents who gave only multiples of 10: {per_resp.mean()*100:.1f}% ({per_resp.sum()} of {len(per_resp)})")

sentences.summary: det_04: Kucharski's own headline findings. Source: Insights from over 150,000 human judgements (Kucharski) (https://kucharski.substack.com/p/insights-from-over-150000-human-judgements) Facts: 'Realistic possibility' had the most variance across respondents; More than half of estimates were multiples of 10; nearly a third ended in 5; ~1 in 5 rounded all estimates

raw_evidence.label: Kucharski's own headline findings
raw_evidence.content: In his write-up, Kucharski reported several patterns the analysis should check against. 'Realistic possibility' showed the most variance — it 'meant a lot of different things to different people' despite the UK's official 40–50% definition. Respondents almost unanimously agreed 'almost no chance' is lower than 'will happen', but split nearly 50/50 on whether 'could happen' or 'might happen' is higher. People love round numbers: more than half of all absolute estimates were multiples of 10, nearly a third ended in 5, and about one in five participants rounded every single estimate. Demographic effects were real but small: Americans gave estimates ~1.03x higher than British respondents, age effects were minimal (55–64 gave ~0.97x vs the 35–44 reference). Kucharski himself questioned whether 1–3% differences, though statistically significant in such a large sample, matter in practice.

raw_evidence.label: Presentation order barely moves the needle
raw_evidence.content: Does the position a phrase appears in nudge how high you rate it? Only faintly. After centering each phrase to remove its own average, the value crept up with position — from about -0.6 points for the first three phrases shown to +0.3 for the last three, a swing of under 1 percentage point across all 19 positions. The correlation between presentation order and the term-centered estimate is just 0.024. So there is a whisper of an anchoring/warm-up effect, but it is far too small to matter for any real decision — a useful myth-buster against the worry that the quiz design biased the answers.

Source: Probability & the words we use: why it matters (Tony Martin-Vegue) (https://www.tonym-v.com/blog/2020/08/09/predictive) Facts: Vague probability words cause real miscommunication in risk and security decisions; Practitioners advocate replacing words with numeric ranges to reduce ambiguity | det_02: Sherman Kent and the 'serious possibility' problem. raw_evidence.label: Why it matters: real-world stakes of vague words
raw_evidence.content: Estimative phrases are not academic. They appear in intelligence assessments that inform war decisions, in IPCC climate reports read by policymakers, in medical consent conversations ('this side effect is common'), in legal standards ('reasonable doubt'), in weather forecasts, and in financial disclosures. When 'likely' can mean 55% to one reader and 90% to another, the same sentence can justify opposite decisions. The 1986 Challenger disaster and various intelligence failures have been linked in part to miscommunicated uncertainty. The dataset's value is that it measures, at population scale, exactly how much ambiguity these everyday words carry — and which ones are most treacherous.

facts: Vague probability words cause real miscommunication in risk and security decisions
Practitioners advocate replacing words with numeric ranges to reduce ambiguity

raw_evidence.label: Sherman Kent and the 'serious possibility' problem
raw_evidence.content: The core problem this dataset probes is decades old. In 1951 a US National Intelligence Estimate said there was a 'serious possibility' of a Soviet attack on Yugoslavia. When CIA analyst Sherman Kent — later called the 'father of intelligence analysis' — polled colleagues on what 'serious possibility' meant numerically, answers ranged from a 20% chance to an 80% chance for the very same phrase. Kent's 1964 essay 'Words of Estimative Probability' argued that verbal probability terms are dangerously ambiguous and proposed a fixed scale mapping words to numbers (e.g. 'probable' = 75% ±12%, 'almost certain' = 93% ±6%, 'chances about even' = 50%). The Kucharski quiz is essentially a crowd-sourced, 5,000-person rerun of Kent's experiment.

raw_evidence.label: Why it matters: real-world stakes of vague words
raw_evidence.content: Estimative phrases are not academic. They appear in intelligence assessments that inform war decisions, in IPCC climate reports read by policymakers, in medical consent conversations ('this side effect is common'), in legal standards ('reasonable doubt'), in weather forecasts, and in financial disclosures. When 'likely' can mean 55% to one reader and 90% to another, the same sentence can justify opposite decisions. The 1986 Challenger disaster and various intelligence failures have been linked in part to miscommunicated uncertainty. The dataset's value is that it measures, at population scale, exactly how much ambiguity these everyday words carry — and which ones are most treacherous.

Practitioners advocate replacing words with numeric ranges to reduce ambiguity

raw_evidence.label: Sherman Kent and the 'serious possibility' problem
raw_evidence.content: The core problem this dataset probes is decades old. In 1951 a US National Intelligence Estimate said there was a 'serious possibility' of a Soviet attack on Yugoslavia. When CIA analyst Sherman Kent — later called the 'father of intelligence analysis' — polled colleagues on what 'serious possibility' meant numerically, answers ranged from a 20% chance to an 80% chance for the very same phrase. Kent's 1964 essay 'Words of Estimative Probability' argued that verbal probability terms are dangerously ambiguous and proposed a fixed scale mapping words to numbers (e.g. 'probable' = 75% ±12%, 'almost certain' = 93% ±6%, 'chances about even' = 50%). The Kucharski quiz is essentially a crowd-sourced, 5,000-person rerun of Kent's experiment.

raw_evidence.label: 'Realistic Possibility' vs the official 40–50%
raw_evidence.content: UK intelligence officially defines 'realistic possibility' as a 40–50% likelihood. The crowd disagrees wildly: only 17.5% of responses landed inside that 40–50% band. Far more (64.0%) placed it above 50%, and 18.5% put it below 40%. The mean was 57.0 and the median 60 — both above the official ceiling. Estimates filled the entire 0–100 range, with a clear peak around 60–70%. In other words, the phrase that a government uses to mean 'a bit less than even' is read by most people as 'better than even'. It is the dataset's sharpest illustration of why a single estimative word cannot safely carry a decision.

print(f"Min {rp.min()} Max {rp.max()}  range spans full 0-100")
# spread histogram for chart
bins = list(range(0, 101, 10))
hist = pd.cut(rp, bins=bins, include_lowest=True).value_counts().sort_index()
print("histogram (10-pt bins):")
for iv, c in hist.items():
    print(f"  {int(iv.left)}-{int(iv.right)}: {c}")

# --- ana_04: How wide each phrase spans — full-range phrases ---
print("=== ana_04 ===")
span = aj.groupby('term')['probability'].agg(['min','max','std'])
span['range'] = span['max'] - span['min']
# fraction of mass in extreme tails for the "spanning" phrases
for t in ['May Happen','Might Happen','Could Happen','Realistic Possibility']:
raw_evidence.output: mean 57.0 median 60 std 20.5; inside 40-50%: 17.5%; below 40%: 18.5%; above 50%: 64.0%; histogram peak 60-70 (1049) and 50-60 (936)
